To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cirrhosis, fibrosis, and carcinoma of the liver may be associated with HBsAg, a1-antitrpsin bodies, or alcohol, singly or in combination, and that copper staining of liver tissue is not a reliable diagnostic method for cirrhosis.

cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinomas are associated with HBsAg in a proportion of cases, and that the presence of HBsAg can be demonstrated in tissue by immunofluorescent and immunoperoxidasemethods, and not by the use of Torcein and Aldehyde Fuchsin staining.
the aetiology of cirrhotic liver disease is alcohol, hepatitis B virus, a1-antirypsin deficiency, and copper.

the aetiology of cirrhotic liver disease.
the histological study of cirrhosis and hepatocellular cancer.
the histological study of the aetiology of cirrhotic liver disease, hepatic fibrosi, and hepatocellu lar carcinoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cirrhosis is due to alcohol, hepatitis B infection, or both, that severe fibrosis is due to alcohol or hepatitis B, and that hepatocellular carcinoma is due to alcohol and/or hepatitis B.
alcohol, HBsAg, and a1-antirrypsin bodies are the three major causes of cirrhosis and that HBsAg is a major cause of hepatocellular cancer.
cirrhosis, fibrosis, and carcinoma are associated with alcohol, HBsAg, or al-antitryp- sin bodies, and that the last association is rare.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
alcohol and HBsAg are the two major aetiological agents of cirrhosis and carcinoma of the liver in this country.
alcohol is the commonest cause of cirrhosis and hepatitis B virus of hepatocellular cancer.

alcohol is the most important aetiological factor, followed by HBsAg, but the relative importance of the two is uncertain; a1-antirypsin deficiency may be of importance in a few cases; copper is of doubtful importance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a single method to detect HBsAg is not adequate for the histological study of cirrhotic, fibrotic, or neoplastic livers.

the liver is a major target organ for the adverse effects of alcohol and that the liver is the primary target for the development of alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis, as well as the most common target for the development and progression of hepatocellular cancer.
the majority of patients with cirrhosis have a known aetiology and that the most common aetiological agents are alcohol and HBsAg.
